title: Paint and clear-coat care
audience: Car detailers who inspect paint and decide whether correction is within scope.
learningOutcomes: Carry out a clean-media wash sequence before any correction.
Inspect the finish under suitable lighting and identify the defect.
Refer uncertain defects and decline aggressive correction that is not agreed.

instruction.heading: Clean before you correct
instruction.body: Correction removes material from the surface, so the surface must be clean first. Grit left on the paint is pushed around by the pad and can leave new marks. The Auto-Detailing guide puts washing ahead of every other step and notes that most swirls come from the wash and dry. Use a two-bucket method: one bucket of shampoo solution and one of clean rinse water with a bucket insert that traps grit at the bottom, and rinse the wash mitt after each panel. Use separate wash media for wheels and tyres, and wash lightly soiled areas before heavily soiled ones. Degrease tar, sap and bird droppings before the shampoo wash, following the degreaser label for dilution and dwell, and rinse the degreaser fully so none remains on the paint. Dry by sheeting the water off and blotting with a clean microfibre towel rather than dragging it across the paint. Only then decontaminate with clay or a decontamination pad (“Clay bar and decontamination”), and check the surface by touch. A paint that still feels rough after the wash is not ready for correction.

instruction.heading: Inspect the finish under suitable light
instruction.body: The inspection decides what correction is needed, so do it properly. Wash in shade, but inspect with a light that shows the surface. A directional torch held low across the panel reveals swirls and water spots that flat light hides. The Spanish-language manual makes the same point, advising a light close to the surface, and the show-car sample describes a baggie test, where a clean plastic bag over the hand makes rough spots easier to feel. Name each defect by type: a fine swirl pattern, a hazed or oxidised surface, water spotting, etching, or a scratch that catches the light. Note the depth where you can. The Auto-Detailing guide says a finishing polish typically will not remove anything deeper than a very light swirl, so a deeper mark needs a different plan. Check each panel separately, because a single car can have different paint on different panels. The show-car sample describes a car that was clear-coated everywhere except the trunk lid, which had single-stage paint, so each panel needs its own check; “Polishing and paint correction: the difference” gives the pad test.

instruction.heading: Deciding whether to correct
instruction.body: After inspection, decide whether correction is appropriate and at what level. Correction means removing a thin layer of clear coat to level the surface. The clear layer on a modern car is thin. The show-car sample gives roughly 50 micrometres (2 mils in its own measurement), though the figure varies between manufacturers. Every cut removes part of a finite layer, so deep work carries real risk. A deep scratch may pass through the clear coat into the colour coat, and aggressive correction can remove too much of what is left. A colleague may propose a compound to chase a deep scratch. Do not start on that suggestion alone. Identify the defect and its depth as well as you can, and refer uncertain defects to a competent specialist or to the owner, with the risk stated. Clear-coat failure, where the clear coat peels or hazes and will not level, cannot be polished out. The show-car sample describes repainting as the only remedy. A detailer records the failure and declines to promise its removal.

instruction.heading: Record, agree and decline
instruction.body: Record each defect with its location, your assessment of its type and depth, and a photograph taken under the same light each time. Agree the correction and its limits with the customer in writing before work starts. State the risk that a deep defect may not be removable without damage, and that the result cannot be guaranteed. Decline aggressive correction that has not been agreed, and record the decline. Claims about the result must be accurate and must not leave out material facts. The ACCC guidance says intent does not matter when a claim misleads, and that leaving out an important detail can itself mislead. A promise that a scratch will be removed, made before any test, is a claim the business may not be able to support.

procedure: Confirm the owner's agreement to the scope, including whether correction is in scope at all.
Wash in shade by the two-bucket method, with separate wash media for wheels and tyres.
Degrease heavily soiled areas, rinse them fully, and dry by sheeting and blotting.
Decontaminate the paint, then recheck the surface by touch.
Inspect each panel under a directional light and name each defect by type and, where possible, depth.
Decide between no correction, a test spot at the least aggressive level, or referral, and record the decision.
Record each defect with a dated photograph, agree the limits in writing, and decline any unagreed aggressive correction.

workedExamples.situation: A nine-year-old dark sedan has a fine swirl pattern on the doors and a deep scratch on the rear quarter panel. A colleague offers a more aggressive compound to take the scratch out.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What happens before any correction starts?
workedExamples.reasoning: Inspect the rear quarter under a directional light and record the scratch's location and depth. Refer the deep scratch to a specialist or the owner, and state the risk of cutting through the clear coat. Do not run the aggressive compound on the scratch without a written agreement and a passing test spot. Agree a limited finishing-level correction on the fine swirls only if the test works. Record the decline of the aggressive correction and the limits in writing.

workedExamples.situation: A silver car has light water spotting on the bonnet and fine swirls on the driver's door. It was washed in direct sun and dried with spots.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the right order of work?
workedExamples.reasoning: Wash again in shade, rinse, and dry by sheeting and blotting. Inspect the bonnet under a directional light and record the spotting as water spotting, not paint damage. Test a finishing-level polish and a fine pad on a small part of the door before the wider area. If the test shows improvement without damage, correct the door at the agreed level and record the result. If the spots do not respond, record that they remain and that the result is limited.

equipmentAndPpe: Directional light (torch) and a second light source for dark finishes.
Camera, used with the owner's permission, and a consistent photo position.
Clean microfibre towels in a dedicated group, and separate wash media for wheels and tyres.
Bucket insert that traps grit, one for each rinse bucket.
Degreaser and polishes used only as their labels direct.
PPE: gloves and eye protection when using machines or chemicals, as each SDS requires. No rings, watches or loose buttons that can scratch the paint.

commonErrors.error: Correcting a panel that is still dirty.
commonErrors.prevention: Clean, decontaminate and recheck by touch before any correction.

commonErrors.error: Relying on flat or overhead light.
commonErrors.prevention: Use a directional light held low across the panel.

commonErrors.error: Promising that a scratch will be removed.
commonErrors.prevention: Describe the likely result and the limits, and put them in writing.

commonErrors.error: Stepping up to a more aggressive product without a test spot.
commonErrors.prevention: Test the least aggressive combination first and record the result.

commonErrors.error: Treating clear-coat failure as a polishing job.
commonErrors.prevention: Record the failure, refer it, and decline correction. Repainting is outside this course.

commonErrors.error: Wearing rings, watches or buttons that scratch paint.
commonErrors.prevention: Remove jewellery and wear clothing without loose buttons near the panel.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Claims about the result of correction must be accurate and supportable, and must not leave out material facts (ACCC: false or misleading claims). The business must be able to back up what it says about results.

Abrasive and polishing products have their own labels and SDSs that govern use. Dilution, dwell time and PPE are not given here: follow each label and SDS. Machine polishers are electrical equipment: check cords and plugs before use, and keep cords off wet ground.

qualityStandard: Surface washed, decontaminated and rechecked by touch before any correction.
Each defect in the case study is named by type, located, and recorded with a photograph under a directional light.
No aggressive correction is started without a written agreement and a passing test spot, and each decline is recorded.
documentationEvidence: Defect record with location, type, depth estimate, and a dated photograph under the same light.
Written agreement of the correction scope and limits, and the record of any decline or referral.
summary: Clean and decontaminate before any correction, and inspect under a directional light.
Name each defect by type; a light swirl and a deep scratch need different plans.
Agree limits in writing, and never promise removal you cannot show.

knowledgeChecks.question: What must happen to the surface before correction?
options: Nothing, since the polish removes all the dirt on its own
Apply wax first so the polish slides across easily
Use a stronger compound to clear the dirt before the wash
Wash, decontaminate and recheck the surface by touch

knowledgeChecks.question: A deep scratch is found on a panel. A colleague suggests the aggressive compound. What is correct?
options: Use it, because the colleague is experienced and knows the product and the paint well today
Refer the defect or record the limits, and get written agreement before any aggressive correction
Use it in a corner nobody will look at, so any mistake is hidden from the owner and the customer
Use it, then tell the customer afterwards, once the result has been checked and it looks fine

knowledgeChecks.question: Which light best reveals swirls and water spots?
options: Flat overhead lighting in the workshop
Direct midday sun on the panel
A phone screen held flat over the panel
A directional light held low across the panel
